subject: chemistry_2
question_text: What are analgesics? How are they classified? Give examples.

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Unit 14 (Chemistry in Everyday Life) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.105-106, printed chapter "11. CHEMISTRY IN EVERYDAY LIFE"; the book prints this question on book p.106 as SAQ 1. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK WORDING (book p.106, SAQ 1): the printed answer reads "The drugs which reduce pain without causing disturbances of nervous system". The standard wording is longer and is used here: without causing loss of consciousness, mental confusion, loss of coordination or any other disturbance of the nervous system. BOOK ERROR: the printed answer says "Narcotic means drowsiness". Narcotic comes from a word meaning to benumb; in medicinal doses these drugs relieve pain and produce sleep, and in large doses they produce stupor, coma and even death. The card gives the effect rather than the false word origin. BOOK SLIP: the printed answer calls heroin an alkaloid along with morphine and codeine. Morphine is an alkaloid obtained from the opium poppy; heroin is diacetylmorphine, made from morphine in the laboratory, so it is a derivative of an alkaloid and not one itself. Codeine is described both ways: it occurs in opium, and it is also made from morphine by methylation. The card writes the three as a group of morphine and its derivatives, which is how the printed lines, the why and the memory tip on this card all read; a Telangana IPE teacher should settle which description of codeine the board's key expects. BOOK GAP: the book never separates an analgesic from an antipyretic, although aspirin and paracetamol are both. That boundary is added on the last step.

steps.label: The definition
lines: Analgesics are drugs that reduce or
remove pain without causing loss of
consciousness, mental confusion, loss of
coordination, or any other disturbance
of the nervous system.
Ex: morphine, aspirin, paracetamol.
steps.why: The whole definition rests on the second half. Any strong drug can stop pain by putting a patient to sleep; an analgesic is defined by removing the pain while leaving the patient awake and able to think and move. That is why the list of things it must not cause is written out.
common_mistakes: Writing only that it reduces pain. The words without disturbing the nervous system are half of this mark.
Confusing an analgesic with a tranquilliser. An analgesic reduces pain; a tranquilliser treats stress.
steps.memory_tip: Pain gone, patient awake: that pair of facts is the definition.
steps.margin_note: Write both halves of the definition. Reduce pain alone is usually half this mark.

steps.label: The two types named
lines: Analgesics are of two types.
The two are separated by whether the
drug is habit forming.
steps.why: The question says "how are they classified", so the two names and the basis of the classification are a mark on their own. The basis is whether the drug is habit forming, and stating it is what turns two labels into a classification.
common_mistakes: Giving the two names with no basis of classification. The words habit forming or addictive are what earn this mark.
Writing three or four types. There are two.
steps.memory_tip: Two types, one test: is the drug habit forming or not?
steps.margin_note: Number the two types and write the basis in one line. The examiner counts two headings here.

steps.label: Narcotic analgesics
lines: Narcotic analgesics: these slow down the
central nervous system.
In medicinal doses they relieve pain and
produce sleep; in large doses they
produce stupor, coma and even death.
They are habit forming, so they are given
only under medical control.
Ex: morphine and its derivatives, heroin
and codeine.
steps.why: Morphine is an alkaloid obtained from the opium poppy, and heroin and codeine are made from it, so the whole group is written as morphine and its derivatives. The doses matter: the same compound relieves pain in a small dose and causes coma in a large one, and that is why these drugs are controlled.
common_mistakes: Writing aspirin here. Aspirin is a non-narcotic analgesic.
Writing that narcotic means drowsiness. It means to benumb; the drowsiness is one effect, not the meaning.
steps.memory_tip: Morphine, heroin, codeine: one parent and its two derivatives, all habit forming.
steps.margin_note: Two examples and the words habit forming finish this mark.

steps.label: Non-narcotic analgesics
lines: Non-narcotic analgesics: these are not
habit forming and are used for mild pain
such as headache and backache.
Aspirin also brings a high temperature
down, so it is an antipyretic as well.
An analgesic reduces pain; an antipyretic
reduces fever. Morphine does only the
first, aspirin does both.
steps.why: Aspirin and paracetamol are the two names every paper expects here. The closing lines separate two classes that students often confuse: an analgesic acts on pain and an antipyretic acts on a raised body temperature. Aspirin belongs to both classes, morphine only to the first, and that pair of facts is what makes the boundary clear.
common_mistakes: Writing that every analgesic reduces fever. Morphine does not; aspirin does.
Writing paracetamol as a narcotic. It is non-narcotic and is not habit forming.
steps.memory_tip: Aspirin reduces pain and also reduces fever; morphine reduces pain only.
steps.margin_note: Two examples finish this mark. The antipyretic line is what separates pain relief from fever relief.

insider_note: Four parts, one mark each: the definition, the two types with the basis, the narcotic group with examples, the non-narcotic group with examples. A student who writes the definition and a list of drug names usually earns two of the four, because the basis of the classification is missing.
